# Diagnosing Random Misfires on a 2012 Mini Cooper S Coupe

Random misfires on a BMW N54/N55 engine platform, specifically in a 2012 Mini Cooper S Coupe, often stem from a convergence of fuel delivery issues and airflow leaks rather than a single catastrophic failure. The symptoms you describedârough cold starts that smooth out after throttle application, combined with P0087 and P15DF codesâare highly indicative of low fuel pressure at startup or an intake leak causing incorrect air-fuel mixture calculations.

The High Pressure Fuel Pump (HPFP) is frequently the culprit behind P0087 (Fuel Rail/System A - Pressure Too Low). This component is notorious for wear on this model year, often failing prematurely due to varnish buildup from degraded fuel or age-related seal degradation. While the HPFP is indeed expensive (often around $650 new), it is a critical safety and performance component that cannot be "cleared" via software adjustments. The only reliable fix is replacement. However, before committing to a full assembly swap, verify the condition of the pump's internal plunger and O-ring seals if you have access to a teardown kit, though this is rarely cost-effective for DIY repairs on high-pressure units.

Simultaneously, the P15DF code usually points to an Ignition Coil performance issue. Your observation that all coils showed a loss of power confirms a systemic ignition weakness. While swapping coils with spark plugs won't fix the coil's internal short or open circuit, replacing both components together is standard practice if the coils are failing simultaneously. This suggests a potential grounding issue in the engine bay or a failing Ignition Control Module (ICM), which controls the firing of these coils.

Airflow integrity is equally critical. You noted that the plastic side intake tube has vibrated loose near the driver's side rear. This is a significant red flag. Even if the vacuum leak seems minor, unmetered air entering the engine after the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor disrupts the lambda sensor readings. The ECU will lean out the mixture in an attempt to compensate, leading to misfires and rough idling. Replacing this tube or securing it with a proper clamp is essential; relying on manual vibration won't restore the seal pressure needed for stable combustion.

Regarding your live data captures showing RPM fluctuations with the AC compressor cycle: this is expected behavior but can be exacerbated by vacuum leaks. If the ECU detects a lean condition (due to the intake leak), it may not compensate fully for the load change caused by the AC clutch engaging, causing further hesitation.

To address the high idle RPM (~700â800 RPM) and cold start struggles, focus on mechanical integrity first. Verify that the throttle body is clean and that there are no stuck valves in the Idle Air Control (IAC) system inherent to this engine architecture. If the misfires persist after replacing the HPFP, coils, plugs, and fixing the intake leak, investigate the fuel pressure regulator or the secondary low-pressure pump in the tank assembly.

Finally, regarding the diagnostic fees: utilizing open-source data logging tools like OBDLink with compatible software (e.g., Carly or Torque Pro) can replicate the Bosch Bluetooth connector diagnostics for free. This allows you to monitor live fuel rail pressure and ignition timing across multiple cylinders without paying a shop for a diagnosis. If the live data shows the fuel rail dropping below 50 bar immediately upon cranking, the HPFP is definitely on its last legs and requires replacement.
